title: An LRU Cache

concept.title: A hash map for finding, a list for the order of use
body: A **cache** keeps a limited number of items in fast memory. When it is full, the **least recently used** (LRU) item is thrown out to make room. Both `get` and `put` must be O(1). Two structures work together: a **hash map** finds an item by its key in O(1), and a **doubly linked list** keeps the items in the order of their last use (the most recent at one end). Moving a node to the front or removing the node at the back are O(1) pointer changes in a doubly linked list.

Rules: `get key` returns the value (or -1 if absent) and makes the key the most recently used. `put key value` stores or updates the value and makes the key the most recently used; if the cache is full and the key is new, the least recently used key is removed first.

body.code:
get:  if key in cache: move to the most recent position; return value; else -1
put:  if key in cache: update, move to the most recent position
      else: if len(cache) == capacity: remove the oldest; insert as the most recent

body: Languages offer shortcuts for the pair "map plus order": in Python the built-in `dict` remembers the insertion order, so `pop` and insert again moves a key to the end, and `next(iter(d))` is the oldest key; Java's `LinkedHashMap` can do the same. In C++ the standard way is `list` plus `unordered_map` of iterators. Building the doubly linked list yourself is a very good exercise.

statement: Implement an LRU cache with the capacity `cap`. Process `n` operations. Each line has an operation and two numbers: `get key 0` prints the value of the key, or -1 if the key is not in the cache, and makes the key the most recently used; `put key value` stores the value (updating it if the key exists) and makes the key the most recently used; if the cache is full and the key is new, the least recently used key is removed first. Print the answer of every `get`.
inputFormat: Each of the next `n` lines has an operation and two numbers.
constraints: There is at least one `get` operation.

examples.input:
8 2
put 1 1
put 2 2
get 1 0
put 3 3
get 2 0
put 4 4
get 1 0
get 3 0
examples.note: After get 1, key 2 is the least recently used and is removed by put 3: get 2 gives -1. Put 4 removes key 1: get 1 gives -1, get 3 gives 3.

hints: You need to find a key quickly and to know which key was used longest ago.
Keep the keys in order of use: the oldest first. On every use, move the key to the end.
When the cache is full and a new key comes, remove the oldest key.

starter.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n, cap = map(int, input().split())
ops = [input().split() for _ in range(n)]

# Your code here

explanation: An ordered map keeps the keys from the least to the most recently used. Every use moves the key to the end; when the cache is full, the first key is removed.
solution.complexity: O(1) per operation on average, space O(cap).
